main.text: [II, 648] [col. 91] Chapter XIV.

The various names of the quail, שלו, سلوي [salwā], سماني [sumānā], ፈርፈርት and the various kinds according to the Hebrews: 1. שיכלי, Συκαλὶς [Sykalis], 2. קכלי, Κίχλη [Kichlē]. 3. פסיוני, the pheasant. 4. שליו.

Of the quails which God generously granted to the Israelites when they were perishing of hunger in the desert, Moses writes thus, Exod. XVI, 13: And it came to pass in the evening that quails came up and covered the camp. And Num. XI, 31: Then a wind going forth from the Lord swept quails from the sea and scattered them over the camp, about a day's journey on this side and about a day's journey on that side, round about the camp, and that to two cubits above the face of the earth. 32. And the people rose up all that day, and all that night, and all the next day, and gathered the quails. He who gathered least gathered ten cors, and they spread them out widely round about the camp. 33. But while the flesh was still between their teeth, not yet chewed, the wrath of the Lord was kindled against the people, and the Lord smote the people with a very great plague. 34. Therefore they called the name of that place kibroth thaava (that is, graves of craving), because there they had buried the people of those who had craved. David also, Psal. LXXVIII, 26: He drove the east wind into the heavens, and by his power he brought in the south wind. 27. And he rained flesh upon them as dust, and winged fowl as the sand of the sea. 28. These he cast into the midst of their camp, round about their tents. 29. And they ate until they were filled, having received from him what they had craved. 30. They had not yet put away their craving, and the food was still in their mouth, 31. when the wrath of God came upon them and slew the fattest of them, and laid low the choicest of Israel. And Psal. CV, 40: When they asked, he brought quails, and satisfied them with the bread of heaven.

The Hebrew name of the quail is שלו selau; the Chaldee is likewise סליו selau; the Syriac ܣܠܘܝ salvai; and the Arabic سلوي [salwā] in the same letters, although they pronounce it selvva. Hence the Qur'an, Azoara 17, entitled اعراف [Aʿrāf] or The Limbo: انزلنا عليهم المن والسلوي [anzalnā ʿalayhim al-manna wa-l-salwā] We sent down upon them manna and quails. Some explain it as honey, because the Arabic word سلوي [salwā] selvva signifies honey as well as quails. Taken in that way, من [mann] manna and سلوي [salwā] selvva would be synonyms. For manna is aerial honey. That is why it is called ἀερόμελι [aeromeli] by the sons of the physicians, and by Amyntas in book 1 of τῶν τῆς Ἀσίας σταθμῶν [tōn tēs Asias stathmōn], cited by Athenaeus, book 11. But Alkazuinius and Ibnobitar do better, who assert انه السماني [annahu al-sumānā] that it is the quail. And Alachphas: هو طاير الذي انزله الله تعالي علي بني اسرايل علي القول المشهور وغلط [huwa ṭāʾir alladhī anzalahu Allāh taʿālā ʿalā banī Isrāʾīl ʿalā al-qawl al-mashhūr wa-ghalaṭa] [II, 649] الهزلي فظنه الغسل [al-Hudhalī fa-ẓannahu al-ghasl] It is the bird which God Most High sent down upon the children of Israel, according to the received opinion. So Alhazelius erred, who thought it was honey. There are some among the Arabs who write that the quail is called سلوي [salwā] لانه يسلي الانسان عن ساير الادام [li-annahu yuslī al-insān ʿan sāʾir al-idām] because it makes a man forget other foods. But the Hebrew is שלו selau, which I think should be referred to the verb שלה sala, although the Masoretes wrote the latter with right-hand Sin and the former with left-hand, διακριτικῶς [diakritikōs]. Properly שלה means to live in peace, and then also to abound. Hence it is often rendered by the Greeks εὐθηνεῖν [euthēnein], and שליה εὐθηνία [euthēnia]. It is therefore most likely that quails are named from abundance, since in warm regions scarcely any bird is more prolific, as will appear from what follows ^{(1)}. Another name of the quail among the Arabs, سماني [sumānā] [II, 650] sumana, is agreed to be derived from fatness, because it is a very fat bird. Hence R. Selomo on Exod. XVI.: השלו מין עוף ושמן מאד, The quail, a species of bird which is very fat. And Kimchi in his Lexicon: הוא שמן מאד, it is very fat. In the Ethiopic Psalter, Psal. CIV, 38, ፈርፈርት፡ phorphorath is the quail, the name of the genus having been transferred, as it seems, to the species ^{(2)}. [col. 93] For among the Talmudists פרפרות parperoth or pharpheroth, ἀρχαϊκῶς [archaikōs], are any delicacies made of small and dainty things, such as used to be served either right at the beginning or at the end of a banquet. Hence in the tractate Berachoth, ch. 6, fol. 42a: ברך על הפרפרות שלפני המזון פטר את הפרפרות שלאחר המזון, He who says the blessing over the pharpheroth (that is, delicacies) that are served before the meal exempts (from the blessing) the pharpheroth that are served after the meal. For one blessing suffices for both. And there the Gloss: ומביאין לפני הם פרפרות להמשיך אכילה כגון פרגיות ודגים ואח״כ מביאין השלחן And they served them pharpheroth (or delicacies) to whet the appetite, such as small birds and fish; then they brought the table, that is, the usual foods.

By the Greek translators שלו selau is rendered not ὄρτυξ [ortyx] coturnix [quail], but ὀρτυγομήτρα [ortygomētra] ortygometra. Thus Exod. XVI, 13. Ἀνέβη ὀρτυγομήτρα [Anebē ortygomētra]. And Num. XI, 31. Ἐξεπέρασεν ὀρτυγομήτραν [Exeperasen ortygomētran]. And in the following verse, Καὶ συνέλεγον τὴν ὀρτυγομήτραν [Kai synelegon tēn ortygomētran]. And Psal. CIV, 40. Ἤιτησαν, καὶ ἦλθεν ὀρτυγομήτρα [Ētēsan, kai ēlthen ortygomētra]. And Apollinaris in his Paraphrase,
Ἦλθε μάλ᾽ αἰτίζουσιν ἀπείριτος ὀρτυγομήτρα. [Ēlthe mal' aitizousin apeiritos ortygomētra.]

[II, 651] And Sap. XVI, 2. Τροφὴν ἡτοίμασας ὀρτυγομήτραν [Trophēn hētoimasas ortygomētran]. And Sap. XIX, 12. Ἀνέβη αὐτοῖς ἐκ θαλάσσης ὀρτυγομήτρα [Anebē autois ek thalassēs ortygomētra]. And Philo, book 1 On the Life of Moses, Ὀρτυγομητρῶν νέφος συνεχὲς ἐκ θαλάττης ἐπιφερόμενον πᾶν τὸ στρατόπεδον ἐπεσκίαζε [Ortygomētrōn nephos syneches ek thalattēs epipheromenon pan to stratopedon epeskiaze]. Nor are there lacking those to whom the ortygometra seems to be a bird different from the quail. Augustine on Exodus, Question 62: To them the ortygometra was given, that is, birds which many Latin translators have rendered quails, although the ortygometra is another kind of bird, though not altogether unlike quails. And long before, the Philosopher, Hist. book 8, ch. 12: Ὅταν δ' ἐντεῦθεν ἀπάρωσιν (οἱ ὄρτυγες) ἥ τε γλωττὶς συναπαίρει, καὶ ἡ ὀρτυγομήτρα, καὶ ὁ ὠτὸς, καὶ ὁ κύγχραμος [Hotan d' enteuthen aparōsin (hoi ortyges) hē te glōttis synapairei, kai hē ortygomētra, kai ho ōtos, kai ho kynchramos]· When they (the quails) depart from here, the lingulaca departs together with them, and the ortygometra, and the otus, and the cynchramus. From these words it is evident that the ortygometra, like the lingulaca, the otus and the cynchramus, is distinguished from the quail. Accordingly, further on in the same place there follows: Ἡ δὲ ὀρτυγομήτρα παραπλήσιος τὴν μορφὴν τοῖς λιμναίοις ἐστὶ [Hē de ortygomētra paraplēsios tēn morphēn tois limnaiois esti]· The ortygometra is similar in form to the marsh birds. And in Athenaeus, book 9, the same bird is described by Alexander of Myndus as τὸ μέγεθος ἡ λίκη τρυγὼν, σκέλη δὲ μακρὰ, δυσθαλπὴς καὶ δειλὴ [to megethos hē likē trygōn, skelē de makra, dysthalpēs kai deilē], of the size of a turtle-dove, with long legs, sensitive to cold and timid. Δυσθαλὴς [Dysthalēs], that is, ill-flourishing, is written there without any sense; but I have emended it to δυσθαλπής [dysthalpēs]. In the opinion of these authors, then, it is plain that the ortygometra differs in species from the quail ^{(3)}. For Hesychius, however, ὀρτυγομήτρα [ortygomētra] is nothing other than ὄρτυξ ὑπερμεγέθης [ortyx hypermegethēs], a very large quail, as if the mother or matrix of the others. So among cicadas there is the τεττιγομήτρα [tettigomētra], among sea-urchins the ἐχινομήτρα [echinomētra], among worms the ἰουλομήτρα [ioulomētra] (in Hesychius written ἰουλυμήτρα [ioulymētra]), among the species of lotus Pliny's λωτομήτρα [lōtomētra], and among cities and villages μητρόπολις [mētropolis] and μητροκωμία [mētrokōmia]. For Jansenius, on the book of Wisdom, ch. 16, gravely errs in holding that the ortygometra is so called as if μέτρον τῆς ὄρτυγος [metron tēs ortygos], as though it were the measure and regulator of the other quails. For the word is not written with ε, ὀρτυγόμετρα [ortygometra], but with η, ὀρτυγομήτρα [ortygomētra], so that it plainly means what we said: mother or matrix of quails. And even from this you may infer that the ortygometra differs from the common quail only in size. Therefore many use ὀρτυγομήτρα [ortygomētra] and coturnix [quail] indiscriminately. Among them is Josephus, who instead of ortygometras has simply ὀρτύγων πλῆθος [ortygōn plēthos], an abundance of quails, book 3, ch. 1. And again in ch. 12: Πίμπλαται τὸ στρατόπεδον ὀρτύγων ἅπαν [Pimplatai to stratopedon ortygōn hapan], The whole camp is filled with quails. Jerome too, who for the word ortygometra, which he retained in the Psalms and in the book of Wisdom, has coturnices [quails] in the Law. And the author of the Mirabilia, among the works of Augustine, book 1, ch. 27, [II, 652] plainly treats these as synonyms when he writes of this miracle: A wind, going forth from the Lord, seized quails across the sea and carried them to the places of the camp. And a little [col. 94] later: Around the places of the camp it set down the ortygometra. Nor was the intention of Aristophanes any different in the Birds, where he would have vows made
Λητοῖ ὀρτυγομήτρᾳ, [Lētoi ortygomētra,]

to Latona the ortygometra, that is, the quail. For Latona, when about to give birth, is fabled to have come to Delos changed into a quail, and the island was therefore called Ortygia, as if the quail's island. Jupiter too is fabled to have lain with her ὄρτυγι εἰκασθείς [ortygi eikastheis]. So the Scholiast on Pindar has it, in the argument of the Pythians. That Pliny and Solinus also counted the ortygometra among the kind of quails is proved by a great man in the Plinianae Exercitationes, p. 182. Nor do I doubt that the same was the view of the Greek translators, of the author of the book of Wisdom, of Philo and of Apollinaris, for whom שלו selau is ὀρτυγομήτρα [ortygomētra]. They preferred this word, however, to the simple ὄρτυξ [ortyx], lest it be thought that God had sent the Israelites common quails, rather than the noblest of them.

This is tolerable, and not to be compared with the absurdities of the masters in the Talmudic tractate Ioma, ch. 8, fol. 75 b, where, by the definition of Rabbi Chanina Barabba, ד׳ מיני סליו הן ואלו הן שיכלי וקיכלי ופסיוני ושליו מעליא דכולהו שיכלי גריעי דכולהו שליו, There are four kinds of quails, namely sicli (that is, συκαλὶς [sykalis], ficedula [fig-pecker]), and kichli (that is, κίχλη [kichlē], turdus [thrush]), and phisioni (φασιανὸς [phasianos], phasianus [pheasant]), and selau (the quail properly so called); of which the most excellent is sicli (the fig-pecker), and the meanest of all selau (the quail properly so called). Hence it is that some interpreters render שלו or שלוים as פסיונין, that is, pheasants. So Jonathan on Exod. XVI, 13: וסליקו פסיינין וחפו ית משריתא, And pheasants came up and covered the camp. And R. Joseph the Blind on Psal. CV, 40: שאלו בסרא ואיתי פסיונין, They asked for meat, and he brought pheasants: evidently, for men born for the belly and the gullet it is not enough that God granted quails to the fathers with a liberal hand; so they chose to add those birds that most delight the palate: fig-peckers, thrushes and pheasants. Among these the fig-pecker leads the line,
The waxen fig-pecker that gleams with its broad loin
in Martial, book 5. Hence Juvenal, Satire 14:
— — — who, from a spendthrift father, learned to scrape truffles, to season a mushroom, and to drown fig-peckers swimming in the same sauce.

It was peculiar to the fig-pecker that gluttons liked the whole of it, not, as with other birds, the rump alone. Gellius, book 15, ch. 8, from Favorinus: The masters of the cookshop and of luxury, etc., deny that any bird except the fig-pecker ought to be eaten whole. [II, 653] Of other birds and fattened fowls, unless so much is served that the guests are filled from the rump and the lower part, they think the banquet mean through scarcity; and that those who eat the upper part of birds and fowls have no palate. Hence Martial, book 3, Epigram 59:
A golden turtle-dove fills you with its huge rump.
And Epigram 81:
And gives the turtle-doves' rumps to his concubine.

After the fig-pecker follows קיכלי, κίχλη [kichlē], the thrush; these birds are often joined as equal, or nearly equal, delicacies. Cornelius Celsus, book 2, ch. 18: Of the birds that rely on flight, the larger give firmer nourishment than the small, such as fig-peckers and the thrush. Suetonius, Tiberius, ch. 42: He gave Asellius Sabinus two hundred thousand sesterces for a dialogue in which he had staged a contest of the mushroom, the fig-pecker, the oyster and the thrush. Plautus in the Captivi, alluding to both birds:
There is need of the Turdetani, need of the Ficedulenses,

But, contrary to the opinion of the Hebrews, those who measure everything by the delights of the palate give first place to the fat thrush. The Scholiast of Aristophanes on the Peace: Αἱ κίχλαι εἶδος στρουθῶν, δοκοῦσι δὲ πρὸς τρυφὴν ἐκ τῶν ἄλλων πτηνῶν περισπούδαστοι εἶναι μᾶλλον· [Hai kichlai eidos strouthōn, dokousi de pros tryphēn ek tōn allōn ptēnōn perispoudastoi einai mallon] Thrushes are a kind of small bird which are sought out above others for delicacies. Horace, book 1, Epist. 15:
He used to say that those who devour their goods are right, since nothing is better than a fat [col. 95] thrush. — — — —
Martial, Xenium 92:
Among birds the thrush, if anyone contends with me as judge, among quadrupeds the hare holds the first glory.
And elsewhere:
Perhaps you like a crown woven of roses or rich nard, but I like a crown made of thrushes.
And again:
There a crown heavy with fat thrushes.
Persius, Satire 6:
Nor skilled to know the delicate savour of thrushes.

That is, not a gourmand, a λίχνος [lichnos], who knows well what flavour thrushes have. So formerly at Athens, when discipline was stricter, the young ^{a)} were not permitted ὀψοφαγεῖν [opsophagein], [II, 654] οὐδὲ κιχλίζειν [oude kichlizein], to eat fish, nor thrushes, that is, to dine delicately. And Pompey, when ill, refused to have a thrush sought from Lucullus, although the physician ordered it, using this famous saying: Οὐκοῦν, εἰ μὴ Λούκουλλος ἐτρύφα, Πομπήϊος οὐκ ἂν ἔζησεν; [Oukoun, ei mē Loukoullos etrypha, Pompēios ouk an ezēsen?] Would Pompey then not live without the luxury of Lucullus? This so pleased Plutarch that he related it at least four times: in the Lucullus, in the Pompey, in the Apophthegmata, and in the book Whether an old man should engage in public affairs.

There remains the pheasant, which in former times seems to have been the very summit of delicacies. Thus, according to Athenaeus, book 14, Ptolemy Physcon, although he kept pheasants in great numbers in Egypt, οὐδὲ φασιανικοῦ ὄρνιθός ποτε γεύσασθαι ὡμολόγησεν, ἀλλ᾽ ὥσπερ τι κειμήλιον ἀνακείμενον εἶχε τοὺς δὲ τοὺς ὄρνιθας [oude phasianikou ornithos pote geusasthai hōmologēsen, all᾽ hōsper ti keimēlion anakeimenon eiche tous de tous ornithas], declared that he had never tasted a pheasant, but kept these birds as a stored-up treasure. So in Capitolinus Pertinax never ate a pheasant (fasianus, for there it is written with f) at a private banquet, nor sent one to anyone. In Lampridius, Alexander Severus served pheasant at his table only on the Kalends of January, at the Hilaria of the Mother of the Gods, at the Apollinarian games, at the feast of Jupiter, at the Saturnalia, and on festival days of that kind. In Vopiscus, the emperor Tacitus served the pheasant bird only on his own birthday and those of his family, and on the most festive days. And, as Ammianus attests in book 2, Julian forbade a pheasant to be demanded or brought in at the banquet of the Caesar. Evidently rarity added value to a bird that was excellent in itself. Petronius in the Satyricon:
The bird sought from Phasian Colchis, And African fowl please the palate, Because they are not easy to get. — — —

The bird sought from Phasian Colchis, that is, the pheasant, fetched from the Phasis, a river of Colchis. For it was brought from there, as the name itself shows. Agatharchides on the Phasis, in Athenaeus, book 9: Πλῆθος δὲ ὀρνίθων τῶν καλουμένων φασιανῶν φοιτᾷ τροφῆς χάριν πρὸς τὰς ἐμβολὰς τῶν στομάτων [Plēthos de ornithōn tōn kaloumenōn phasianōn phoita trophēs charin pros tas embolas tōn stomatōn]; A great multitude of the birds they call pheasants resorts to the mouths of the river for the sake of food. Petronius likewise elsewhere:
— — — — Now the Phasis' wave Is bereft of its birds. — — — —
Martial in the Xenia:
I was first carried over in the Argive keel: Before that nothing was known to me but the Phasis.
Statius in The Parrot of Melior, book 2 of the Silvae:

Whom neither the Junonian bird with jewelled tail Could surpass in beauty, nor the bird of the icy Phasis. [II, 655] Clement in the Paedagogus, book 2, ch. 1: Ὄρνεις ἐπὶ τούτοις συνωνοῦνται ἀπὸ Φάσιδος [Orneis epi toutois synōnountai apo Phasidos]; Besides, they buy up birds from the Phasis. Apollonius in Philostratus, book 8, ch. 3: Οὐ κρίνω τοὺς τρυφῶντας ὑπὲρ τοῦ φοινικέου ὄρνιθος, οὐδ' ὑπὲρ τοῦ ἐκ Φάσιδος, ἢ Παιόνων [Ou krinō tous tryphōntas hyper tou phoinikeou ornithos, oud' hyper tou ek Phasidos, ē Paionōn]; I do not bring to judgement those given to luxury on account of the crimson bird (the flamingo), nor on account of the bird from the Phasis or from the Paeonians, that is, the pheasant or the crane. Jordanes, On the Affairs of the Goths, ch. 21: To the river Phasis, from which the Phasian birds have come forth that abound throughout the whole world at the banquets of the powerful. Eustathius on Dionysius: Οἱ φασιανοὶ δὲ τὸ ὄρνεον ἐκεῖθεν παρονομασθῆναι δοκοῦσιν ὡς αὐτόθι πλεονάσαντες [Hoi phasianoi de to orneon ekeithen paronomasthēnai dokousin hōs autothi pleonasantes]; The pheasants, a species of bird, seem to have had their [col. 96] name from there, as having abounded in that place. These things, however commonplace, nevertheless escaped the Talmudists and the Chaldee paraphrasts. For they would not have taken for pheasants the birds that the south wind had brought into the camp of the Israelites, had they known that pheasants are brought from the north. I admit, indeed, that pheasants are not sought from Colchis alone. For to Ptolemy, king of Egypt, ἐκ Μηδείας μετεπέμποντο [ek Mēdeias metepempontō], they were fetched from Media, as Athenaeus testifies in the place cited above. And in the province of Ergimul, Paulus Venetus, book 1, ch. 62, describes very large pheasants, having tails ten or eight palms long. But like Colchis and Media, Ergimul too faces the north, for it is part of Tartary. It seems to be the جرمق [jrmq] giormok of the Arabs, because the name is close and in both places there is musk. See the Nubian Geographer, section 9, Clim. 3. The pheasant is called by another name τατύρας [tatyras] tatyras. So testify Hesychius, and Athenaeus in book 9, following Pamphilus of Alexandria in his Glossary and Epaenetus in his Opsartyticus. I have thought this worth noting because the Persian name of the pheasant, تذرو [tadhrū] tazeru, and the Arabic تدرج [tadruj] tadrug, allude to it.

notes.text: Since the other name of quails, سماني [sumānā], has plainly been given them from their fatness, as Bochart presently notes, ALB. Schultens, in Originib. Hebr. book 1, ch. 3, §39, p. 231, believes that these birds were also called שלו, سلوي [salwā], from that same quality; there he shows that the root سلي [s-l-y], שלה, also contains the notion of rich and fat. — HIOB Ludolf (in Commentar. ad Histor. Aethiop. on book 1, ch. 13, no. 96, p. 172, and in Adpend. ad Histor. Aethiop.), having come upon a passage of Porphyry, περὶ ἀποχῆς ἐμψυχῶν [peri apochēs empsychōn] book 1, §2, where he says that an army in Africa suffering from famine was saved by the arrival of locusts, contends that the שלוים are locusts. For it is well known that locusts are a very common food in almost the whole of the East. The Jews living in Arabia today also think that the שלוים are locusts, and Niebuhr himself agrees with them, Beschreib. von Arab. p. 172. But the strongest objection is that in the Arabic, Syriac and Chaldee dialects this word without any doubt means quails. Nor is שלו found among the names of locusts in Levit. XI, 22. More has been noted by I. E. Faber, ad Harmar. 2, p. 427, and Oedmann in the Vermischten Sammlungen vol. 4, ch. 6, p. 58. — That the שלוים are flying fish, met with in the Red Sea, which the inhabitants of those lands are also accustomed to eat (cf. Hasselquist p. 255; Niebuhr Beschreib. von Arab. p. 176; Forsskål Descriptt. Animal. p. 16), was formerly the conjecture of OL. RUDBECK (Ichthyol. Bibl. Specim. I.), which I. D. Michaelis elaborated further in his Commentat. super lege Mosaica Deut. XXII, 6. 7. §9, and in the Addition to §9, in Syntagm. Commentatt. vol. 2, p. 104 and 115; afterwards, however, he himself rejected it, and rightly so, since in the Red Sea there is no such abundance of flying fish that many thousands of people could be fed with them daily. Nor can these fish rise more than three or four feet above the sea. In addition, flying fish are not an ordinary food; rather, dried, they serve as a medicine for strengthening the stomach. Cf. Niebuhr p. 177. For other points see Faber and Oedmann, loc. cit. — The Seleucid birds [Turdus Seleucis Forsskål vol. 6 a, p. 5, no. 16, Arabic سمرمر [samarmar], Turdus roseus Linnaeus 2, p. 819, no. 15, 13th ed.; Oedmann 2, ch. 6, p. 103], whose coming (as Pliny reports, Hist. Nat. 10, ch. 26, sect. 39) the inhabitants of Mount Casius obtain by prayer from Jupiter when locusts are ravaging their crops; it has not been discovered where they come from or where they go, and they are never seen except when their protection is needed, were suspected by [II, 650] HERMANN VON DER HARDT to be the same as the שלוים; RATHLEF also fought for this opinion in his Append. Acridotheol., but with futile arguments, which I. D. Michaelis long ago refuted in the commentary cited, p. 104 ff. — There is a bird, common in Syria, Arabia and Egypt, of the size of a partridge or turtle-dove, of the grouse family, with hard and dry flesh, which the Arabs, from the call it utters, call قَطًّا [qaṭṭan] Katta (as Hasselquist and Russell write it) (see Golius's Lexic. p. 1934, where a description of this bird is also found); in Linnaeus it is Tetrao supra varius; rectricibus duabus intermediis duplo longioribus subulatis, see Syst. Nat. vol. 1, part 2, p. 754, no. 11, under the heading Alchata, where the synonyms and those who have treated of it are also listed. That this bird is the שלו of the Hebrews is so certain to Hasselquist that in his Travels p. 333, after describing it fairly accurately under the name Tetrao Israelitarum, he uses these words: this, if any, is the bird taken as food by the Israelites in the desert, since it is common in the places through which they wandered. But this very point holds also of the quail, and what is read of the שלוים in Moses does not fit any other bird, as we shall see in the following Chapter. — I. E. Faber, ad Harmar. 2, p. 442, thinks the Arabs' Katta is the same as the quail, though these birds are carefully distinguished by all who have written on the natural history of birds.
The Arabs' فُرْفُر [furfur] and فُرْفُور [furfūr] seem to agree with the Ethiopic word; Golius, in his Lexicon p. 1773, on the authority of Firuzabadi, says it is the name of some bird.

The ὀρτυγομήτρα [ortygomētra] of Aristotle and Athenaeus is the Rallus alis rufo-ferrugineis of Linnaeus, or Crex (Syst. vol. 1, part 2, p. 711), in French Roi de cailles, in German Wiesenschnarre or Wachtelkönig. At Alexandria this bird is today called سلوى [salwā], according to Niebuhr, p. 176, Descr. Arab. But I think that the Greek translators understood by ὀρτυγομήτραις [ortygomētrais] rather very large quails, which Bochart considers probable; read what follows from him.
